body:
## Why

Today a budget tier is a **target**. The coordinator turns the user's budget rules into a tier, value, mid-range, or posh, for each stay's lodging and each meal stop, and stores it with the rule that produced it. A worker then searches at that tier, and code copies the tier onto each candidate (technical spec section 9). Real budget rules don't fit three boxes. On Joe's Natick to Bar Harbor trip (session `session_5hf47qpn`), the budget rules were:

> "Meals: upscale or posh, we are foodies and willing to splurge on good food, especially lobster when we are in Maine. Something mid-tier for the hotel in Bar Harbor. OK to do upscale for hotel in Camden and Portland, a B&B could be a good option in one of them."

The coordinator stored posh, with the rule "meals upscale or posh", on every meal stop, the 7 a.m. coffee stops included. It stored "upscale hotel or B&B" as the rule for both Camden and Portland. Each of those lost what the user meant:

- "Foodies willing to splurge on good food" is about quality, not how fancy a place is. The best lobster roll in Maine likely comes from a shack with counter service, which is value. A worker told to search at posh would skip it.
- What the coffee stops need is good espresso, open by 7 a.m. A tier says neither.
- "A B&B could be a good option in one of them" became a B&B target for both stays.

So the tier becomes a **label**: what a place is like, judged by the worker for each candidate and shown on its card. What a worker aims for comes from the user's own words in its worker brief. The budget item goes too. That text was really two things: how the user likes to eat, spending included, and what they want from places to stay. So it becomes a **lodging preferences** item, beside meal preferences. That drops the stored target tiers and their rules, which are mostly deterministic code with fiddly rules, and keeps the part that shows agent behavior: reading the user's messy budget words. Decided by Joe in chat on 2026-10-27, while settling #60's open question on budget tiers.

The top tier is also renamed from posh to **upscale**, the word users say. Otherwise the user, the cards, and the coordinator's tools would use two names for one tier, and the trace would too.

## Decided

Decided by Joe in chat on 2026-10-27:

- **A tier says what a place is like,** not how it compares with its neighbors. Value is simple and clean: a budget chain motel, such as a Super 8, or a basic independent motel; counter service, a diner, or a food truck. Mid-range is comfortable, with more service: a mainstream chain hotel, such as a Hampton Inn or a Courtyard, or a well-reviewed independent inn; a typical sit-down restaurant. Upscale: a boutique hotel, a resort, or a top-rated inn or B&B; a chef-driven restaurant where a reservation is wise. For restaurants, Google's price level is a guide, not a rule: $ usually means value, $$ mid-range, $$$ or more upscale. When it's missing, or disagrees with what the place is like, the description decides.
- **Each lodging and meal candidate a worker finds carries its own tier,** judged by the worker. The card shows it. A place the user names has none, and its card shows "your choice", as now. Attractions have no tier, as now. #60 adds the worker tools that take it: `add_lodging_candidates` and `add_stop_candidates`, with a required tier for each lodging or meal candidate.
- **Stays and meal stops no longer have a tier or a tier rule.** That removes: the tier and rule inputs on `add_stay`, `update_stay`, `add_stops`, and `update_stop`; the rule that every meal stop needs a tier; copying the tier onto candidates; "a tier already set isn't revisited"; and `select_candidate` changing the stop's or stay's tier.
- **The trip brief's budget item is replaced by a lodging preferences item.** `defaultTier` and `budgetRulesText` go away, and the trip brief gets `lodgingPreferencesText`: what the user wants from places to stay, in their words, required, like meal preferences. Spending on food goes in meal preferences. On the Bar Harbor trip, "foodies, willing to splurge on good food, especially lobster" is a meal preference, and "something mid-tier for the hotel in Bar Harbor, upscale OK in Camden and Portland, a B&B could be a good option in one of them" is a lodging preference. A preference for free activities goes in interests, since attractions have no tier. A total trip budget, such as "under $3,000", has no item: the app never shows prices (functional spec 7.1), so the coordinator says it can't plan to one. A lodging wish that comes up later in chat, after discovery, goes in trip memory, and a standing one in user memory, as usual.
- **"Higher tier" and "Lower tier" on a card become requests to the coordinator,** such as "something nicer than these." The coordinator reads the stop or stay, and sends a worker with that ask. Nothing is stored. The option cards aren't built yet, so only the docs change for them.
- **The worker brief carries the user's words that apply,** in place of a tier and a rule (technical spec 5.3): the meal or lodging preferences, the interests, and any trip or user memory that fits the stop or stay. The coordinator can add its own reading where a preference is clear, such as "the user wants mid-range for stays of 2+ nights, and this stay is 3 nights." It also keeps track of a wish that covers more than one stay. Example: "a B&B in one of them" goes to both the Camden and Portland researchers, until the user picks a B&B in one of the towns.
- **"Hotels only" means lodging businesses listed on Google,** B&Bs and inns included (functional spec 7.2). It rules out private rentals and campgrounds, which the user can still name (functional spec 7.6).

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md) 5.2 (the trip brief's items), 7.1 (budget tiers and rules), 7.2 (lodging), 7.5 (option cards), and scenario S6.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md) sections 2 (the decision that a worker gets a tier, never the rule text), 4.2 (the refine round), 5.2 (the coordinator's instructions on budget tiers), 5.3 (worker briefs), and 9 (budget tiers).
- [Domain model](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/domain-model.md): the trip brief, stay, stop, and candidate, and the services that set tiers. The tier comes up in about 45 places, including the class diagram and the example trips in section 5.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md) 2.1, for the tools above, and what a read shows of a tier.
- `src/domain/tier.ts` holds the tiers, `TIERS`, and how people say each one, `TIER_WORDS`. `grep -rli tier src web/src` lists the code that uses them.

## Do

- Change the design docs above to the decisions. Don't change `plan/`, `research/`, or `reviews/`, which are records.
- Change the code to match: the domain objects and services, the tools and their input schemas, the itinerary reads, the persistence schemas, and the itinerary view's budget line. Rename the tier `posh` to `upscale`. Fix the tests and the fakes.
- Change the coordinator's prompt: the trip brief's items, and the stay and meal guidance on tiers. The implementer drafts the wording, and Joe reviews it in the PR. Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.
- **No migration.** Saved trips start over instead. Joe decided on 2026-10-27 that the trips saved so far, his own test trips, aren't worth carrying over. Once the PR is merged and deployed, delete every trip, on the server and in the local database, so its transcripts, sessions, trip memory, and places go with it ([persistence design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/persistence.md), section 6, which says what deleting a trip removes. `TripWriter.deleteTrip()` does it). User memory stays, since it isn't part of any trip. On 2026-10-27 the server had three trips: Natick to Bar Harbor, San Francisco to Los Angeles, and one with no focus yet. The Bar Harbor budget text is quoted above, so nothing this issue needs is lost.

## Done when

- `npm run check` passes.
- `grep -rni posh src design web/src` finds nothing.
- No trips are left on the server or in the local database, and a new trip can be started on the server.
- In a chat with the coordinator, it asks about lodging preferences in discovery, saves them and meal preferences in the user's words, and adds stays and meal stops with no tier.

## Ends in

A PR.

## Settled in

The PR. Propose each answer in the PR's decisions comment, and Joe agrees by approving the PR.

## Why

Today a budget tier is a **target**. The coordinator turns the user's budget rules into a tier, value, mid-range, or posh, for each stay's lodging and each meal stop, and stores it with the rule that produced it. A worker then searches at that tier, and code copies the tier onto each candidate (technical spec section 9). Real budget rules don't fit three boxes. On Joe's Natick to Bar Harbor trip (session `session_5hf47qpn`), the budget rules were:

> "Meals: upscale or posh, we are foodies and willing to splurge on good food, especially lobster when we are in Maine. Something mid-tier for the hotel in Bar Harbor. OK to do upscale for hotel in Camden and Portland, a B&B could be a good option in one of them."

The coordinator stored posh, with the rule "meals upscale or posh", on every meal stop, the 7 a.m. coffee stops included. It stored "upscale hotel or B&B" as the rule for both Camden and Portland. Each of those lost what the user meant:

- "Foodies willing to splurge on good food" is about quality, not how fancy a place is. The best lobster roll in Maine likely comes from a shack with counter service, which is value. A worker told to search at posh would skip it.
- What the coffee stops need is good espresso, open by 7 a.m. A tier says neither.
- "A B&B could be a good option in one of them" became a B&B target for both stays.

So the tier becomes a **label**: what a place is like, judged by the worker for each candidate and shown on its card. What a worker aims for comes from the user's own words in its worker brief. That drops the stored target tiers and their rules, which are mostly deterministic code with fiddly rules, and keeps the part that shows agent behavior: reading the user's messy budget words. Decided by Joe in chat on 2026-10-27, while settling #60's open question on budget tiers.

The top tier is also renamed from posh to **upscale**, the word users say. Otherwise the user, the cards, and the coordinator's tools would use two names for one tier, and the trace would too.

## Decided

Decided by Joe in chat on 2026-10-27:

- **A tier says what a place is like,** not how it compares with its neighbors. Value is simple and clean: a budget chain motel, such as a Super 8, or a basic independent motel; counter service, a diner, or a food truck. Mid-range is comfortable, with more service: a mainstream chain hotel, such as a Hampton Inn or a Courtyard, or a well-reviewed independent inn; a typical sit-down restaurant. Upscale: a boutique hotel, a resort, or a top-rated inn or B&B; a chef-driven restaurant where a reservation is wise. For restaurants, Google's price level is a guide, not a rule: $ usually means value, $$ mid-range, $$$ or more upscale. When it's missing, or disagrees with what the place is like, the description decides.
- **Each lodging and meal candidate a worker finds carries its own tier,** judged by the worker. The card shows it. A place the user names has none, and its card shows "your choice", as now. Attractions have no tier, as now. #60 adds the worker tools that take it: `add_lodging_candidates` and `add_stop_candidates`, with a required tier for each lodging or meal candidate.
- **Stays and meal stops no longer have a tier or a tier rule.** That removes: the tier and rule inputs on `add_stay`, `update_stay`, `add_stops`, and `update_stop`; the rule that every meal stop needs a tier; copying the tier onto candidates; "a tier already set isn't revisited"; and `select_candidate` changing the stop's or stay's tier.
- **The trip brief's budget item becomes the user's words.** It replaces the default tier and the budget rules text, and stays required. Examples: "mid-range in general, but we splurge on good food", or the Bar Harbor text above.
- **"Higher tier" and "Lower tier" on a card become requests to the coordinator,** such as "something nicer than these." The coordinator reads the stop or stay, and sends a worker with that ask. Nothing is stored. The option cards aren't built yet, so only the docs change for them.
- **The worker brief carries the user's words that apply,** for budget, meals, and lodging, in place of a tier and a rule (technical spec 5.3). The coordinator can add its own reading where a rule is clear, such as "the user wants mid-range for stays of 2+ nights, and this stay is 3 nights." #60 writes the worker brief, and settles where a lodging preference such as "a B&B in Camden" is kept.
